newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. Fed seen on hold in Feb despite jobs.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. Fed seen on hold in Feb despite jobs.

text.p: Most U.S. economists expect Federal Reserve policy makers to keep short-term interest rates unchanged in February despite evidence the labor market tightened in December, a Reuters poll showed.

Twenty-seven of 29 economists surveyed Friday morning projected no change in the key federal funds rate or the discount rate at the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on February 4 and 5.
But any stronger-than-expected inflation data before the meeting could change that outlook, some economists cautioned.

Only one respondent said the central bank will raise the fed funds target rate to 5.5 percent from its current 5.25 percent at the February meeting, and another expert said the odds for a credit tightening at that time were now 50-50.

U.S. payrolls expanded by 262,000 last month compared with an increase of 127,000 the month before, the Labor Department reported Friday. Wall Street economists in an earlier poll had projected a smaller rise of 192,000.
In addition, the unemployment rate dipped to 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent in November, and average hourly earnings rose 0.5 percent to $12.05.
Experts generally said the jobs data, along with other recent economic news, portrayed swift growth last quarter but were not inflationary enough to bring about a Fed move next month.
"At this point, (the Fed) is probably not quite there yet," said William Dudley, managing director and head of U.S. economic research at Goldman, Sachs and Co Inc.
However, "if the economic news remained on the firm side, you couldn't rule out a tightening in February," he added.
Key inflation reports over the next couple of weeks, such as the Consumer Price Index and the Employment Cost Index, could bring about tighter credit if they are surprisingly strong, Dudley said.
Mostly, the economists said central bankers would wait for confirming data over the next couple of months before deciding to tighten credit.
Eleven respondents projected an interest rate hike sometime in the first quarter, with nine saying it would come in March. Five experts projected no move for the foreseeable future.
Other responses varied widely, with four pundits calling for an easing of credit sometime in 1997.
The yearend economic speedup implied in the December employment report is a temporary blip, said economists calling for an ease or no move.
Philip Braverman, chief economist at DKB Securities Corp, said recent consumer spending trends do not support the Fed embarking on a tightening cycle.
"The underpinning in sales does not seem to support the momentum suggested by today's employment report," said Braverman, who projected an ease in the second quarter.
Full results of the survey follow.
